turns.t: Hello, doctor. I'm Gail, Ruby's foster carer. We've had her since she was three weeks old, and the health visitor sent us. ~
Welcome, Gail. And hello Ruby! Who's the little one with the big eyes? Tell me what the health visitor was worried about. ~
Ba ba. ~
She isn't putting on weight, doctor. She's nine months and she's been flat for about two months, on the chart, I mean.
Flat, meaning her line's stopped climbing?
Yes, it's levelled off. And she's so hungry, she takes every bottle, but it doesn't seem to go on her.
How is she feeding at the moment? Milk and solids? ~
Formula, six bottles a day, and she's started on porridge and fruit. She's never refused anything. ~
Good. Any vomiting after feeds?
No, she doesn't vomit. Well, no, not now. She was sicky when she was tiny.
What do you mean by sicky when she was tiny?
She had reflux, they said. It settled a bit at about four months.
Okay. Any loose stools, runny poos, or poos that smell very bad?
No, nothing runny. Normal nappies, I'd say, no problem.
Is she on any medicine, drops, anything?
Vitamin D drops, 400 units, once a day. That's all.
Good. What do you know of her birth?
She was born at 34 weeks. A few weeks in the special care unit. And her tongue-tie was snipped at two weeks old, before we got her.
That's very helpful. I'll have a look at her. Can you pop her on the couch? ~
There you go, sweetheart. ~
Aaah. ~
Ruby, you're lovely. Let me listen, and feel her tummy.
Is she okay? ~
She looks well, she's alert, and she smiles at me. I don't see anything worrying on the outside. ~
It's just she's not growing. ~
I understand. I can't rule out milk protein intolerance, because it can cause poor weight gain even without vomiting.
What would that mean? ~
It means her body might not be taking up the milk well. It's treatable, and there are different milks, but I want to check first, rather than guess. ~
What checks? ~
I'd like to arrange some blood tests, to look for anaemia and check her nutrition and her gut.
Will she need a needle? ~
Yes, a tiny one, in her hand. I'll book it with the children's nurse, and we'll ring you with results. ~
I'll hold her. ~
And in the meantime, offer her solids before the bottle, so she's hungry for them, and write down everything she eats for a week.
I can do a diary. Will that help? ~
It'll help a lot. Bring it when we see you. ~
Thank you, doctor. I've been so worried that I'm doing something wrong. ~
You're doing a very good job. She's lucky to have you. ~
